stem: Which set of four features does Module 1 say shows up across the seven risk families?
option_A: Passwords, updates, backups and filters
option_B: Speed, volume, cost and location
option_C: Strangers, screens, games and money
option_D: Pressure, secrecy, a request, and a move somewhere more private
rationale: The kit teaches the pattern, not the app. Pressure, secrecy, a request and a move somewhere more private recur whether the setting is a game, a chat or a feed.
kit_source: Academy Module 1, Part 1 (The thread that connects them)

stem: What is the Hackles routine?
option_A: Hackles up? Pause. Check. Tell.
option_B: Look. Listen. Learn.
option_C: Block. Delete. Forget.
option_D: Stop. Drop. Roll.
rationale: Notice the feeling, do nothing yet, check whether it is real and who is asking, then tell a trusted adult.

stem: Why does Module 1 say the old 'stranger danger' slogan is not enough online?
option_A: Strangers are never a danger to children online
option_B: Only adults who are strangers can cause online harm
option_C: Much online harm starts with accounts that look like peers or people a child half-knows, so children need to notice pressure, secrecy and requests whoever is asking
option_D: Children cannot tell who is a stranger, so they should avoid all online contact
rationale: The skill taught is noticing the pattern and telling. The slogan misses accounts that seem friendly and familiar.
kit_source: Academy Module 1, 'A word about stranger danger'

stem: Which figure did Module 1 report for NCMEC's 2025 count of financially motivated sextortion reports?
option_A: More than 500,000, up from more than 360,000
option_B: More than 5,000, up from more than 3,600
option_C: About 80,000, a rise of 37 percent
option_D: More than 50,000, up from more than 36,000 the year before
rationale: These are the counts verified on NCMEC's own page. The 80,000 and 37 percent figures could not be found on the primary pages and were removed from the kit.
kit_source: Academy Module 1, Calm Fact 2; Fact-Check Report Round 1, items 4.1 to 4.4

stem: A colleague drafting a newsletter wants to write 'sextortion reports rose 37 percent.' What is the best advice?
option_A: Give the counts from NCMEC's page (more than 50,000 in 2025, more than 36,000 in 2024) and avoid a percentage the primary pages do not state
option_B: Keep 37 percent because several news sites use it
option_C: Round the rise up to 40 percent so it has impact
option_D: Drop all numbers and say reports are 'exploding'
rationale: The kit's check found the 37 percent figure only in snippets, and the counts imply about 39 percent. Quote the counts from the primary source.
kit_source: Evidence file, Section 2.1; Fact-Check Report Round 1, item 4.2

stem: Why does Module 1 call children not telling 'the most important number for teachers'?
option_A: It shows that lessons are unnecessary
option_B: It proves that children cannot be trusted to report
option_C: It shows that most children are being harmed
option_D: It shows the most powerful thing to teach is that telling is safe, never gets you in trouble, and brings help
rationale: The point is help-seeking. Shame and fear of blame keep children silent, so the lesson design aims at telling.

stem: A candidate wants to quote 'one-third of children told no one and only 3 percent went to police or a helpline.' Which handling is best?
option_A: Say the figures come from UNICEF's first 13 countries (Africa and Southeast Asia), not the US, and confirm them in the primary reports before quoting [VERIFY]
option_B: Present them as US figures because the topic is the same
option_C: Quote them as exact and universal
option_D: Add that 97 percent of US children tell a parent
rationale: Module 1 states the geographic limit. The Round 1 report could not confirm the figures on the project page, so they stay marked for checking.
kit_source: Academy Module 1, Calm Fact 4; Fact-Check Report Round 1, item 4.11

stem: What does the Finkelhor and colleagues (2021) review, as summarized in Module 1, suggest about lesson types?
option_A: One large assembly is the best-supported approach
option_B: Lectures on rules outperform role-play
option_C: Active, skill-based, repeated programs are better supported than one-off assemblies or information-only lessons
option_D: Fear-based warnings are proven to work best
rationale: The summary table in Module 1 favors active, structured, repeated programs. The kit marks the citation [VERIFY] until read in full.
kit_source: Academy Module 1, 'What the research says works'

stem: Which statement is an honest caveat about the evidence for Hackles-style teaching?
option_A: A large randomized trial proves the program prevents sextortion
option_B: Every claim in the kit has been independently verified
option_C: Much of the best evidence comes from an adjacent field, and no rigorous trial of a modern K-12 sextortion or deepfake curriculum is known
option_D: Evidence for fear appeals in online safety is conclusive
rationale: Module 1 and the Assessment Pack both say plainly that no rigorous trial is known and that adjacent-field evidence is used.

stem: Your principal says, 'One big assembly and we are done for the year.' Which reply fits Module 1?
option_A: Refuse and explain that assemblies are harmful
option_B: Affirm the goal, then offer both/and: a short kickoff plus ten short classroom lessons, and offer to pilot with one grade
option_C: Tell the principal the evidence proves assemblies never work
option_D: Agree, since any program is better than none
rationale: Both/and keeps the visible response the principal wants and adds repeated skill practice. Overstating the evidence would not be honest.

stem: A fourth grader says, 'I play every night with a guy named Max. He's 14. He gave me free coins.' What is the best first response?
option_A: Stay calm and curious ('Tell me more about the game'), do not interrogate, make a quiet note and let the counselor know per school process
option_B: Ask the child to show you the whole chat on their device
option_C: Ignore it, because it is just a game
option_D: 'That is dangerous! Never talk to him again!'
rationale: One comment alone is not a disclosure of harm. Gifts, an older 'friend' and nightly contact are a pattern worth noting. Alarm or interrogation ends the conversation.

stem: In the Max scenario, which added detail would change your response to treating it as a possible disclosure?
option_A: The child says other students also have game friends
option_B: The child says Max asked for secrecy, pictures, or a move to a private app, or made threats
option_C: The child says Max is good at the game
option_D: The child says the coins were colorful
rationale: Secrecy, pictures, threats or a move to a private app are the signals the kit says to treat as a potential disclosure and handle with the First 10 Minutes.

stem: Which of these is NOT part of a teacher's role in Hackles?
option_A: Reporting as required
option_B: Noticing and listening
option_C: Handing off to trained people
option_D: Investigating who did it and confronting a suspect
rationale: The role is recognition and response. Investigation, confrontation, viewing images, searching phones and counseling are not the teacher's job.

stem: Why does Module 1 say 'fear without a skill is just fear'?
option_A: A child told only that dangers exist has nothing to do with that information, while a rehearsed skill gives them an action
option_B: Skills make fear unnecessary for adults
option_C: Children cannot feel fear about technology
option_D: Fear is never present in children
rationale: The first reason in 'Why not just scare them' is that fear needs a doable action attached to it.

stem: Module 1 Calm Fact 1 says most children use technology safely most of the time. What follows for teaching?
option_A: Build skills calmly for the minority of moments that go wrong, rather than skipping lessons or using scare tactics
option_B: Assume every child is already being harmed
option_C: Skip online safety lessons
option_D: Teach with graphic stories so the minority takes it seriously
rationale: The fact supports calm skill-building. The existence of serious cases is the reason to teach at all.
kit_source: Academy Module 1, Calm Fact 1; self-check Q2

stem: Which message is a well-formed skill message?
option_A: 'Hackers are everywhere.'
option_B: 'Everyone online is lying.'
option_C: 'Never share anything online.'
option_D: 'If an account asks for your password or code, hackles up: pause and check with a trusted adult.'
rationale: A good skill message names a signal, one concrete action and a person to tell, in a hopeful, shame-free tone.

stem: An article says Thorn found that about 1 in 25 teens have had deepfake nudes created of them. What does the kit's check say?
option_A: The article is right; Thorn's figure is 1 in 25
option_B: Thorn reported 1 in 17 teens; '1 in 25' is the UNICEF figure for some countries, so the article's attribution is wrong
option_C: Thorn's figure is 1 in 8, which is the same thing
option_D: Neither organization has reported such a figure
rationale: Round 1 corrected this exact error: 1 in 17 (Thorn, 1,200 US young people) and 1 in 8 who know someone targeted; 1 in 25 is UNICEF in some countries.

stem: Which sentence for a parent handout is the most defensible?
option_A: 'Every statistic in this handout is guaranteed accurate.'
option_B: 'Studies show Hackles prevents sextortion.'
option_C: 'Research proves fear-based warnings backfire in online safety.'
option_D: 'The evidence on fear appeals is mixed, and direct evidence for online safety is thin, so we teach calm skills with practice.'
rationale: The kit says not to claim fear appeals are proven to backfire in this field and that no trial shows the program prevents harm.

stem: In the kit's rule of thumb for a passphrase, what is the minimum?
option_A: One clever word with symbols
option_B: Five or more unrelated words, at least 15 characters in total, ideally chosen at random
option_C: A pet's name plus the year
option_D: Any eight characters changed monthly
rationale: NIST SP 800-63B-4 sets 15 characters as the minimum for a password used alone. CISA suggests 5 to 7 words and 16 or more characters.
kit_source: Academy Module 2, Part 1; Fact-Check Report Round 1, items 6.1 and 6.2

stem: According to Module 2, which habit matters most?
option_A: Changing it every week
option_B: Sharing it with a trusted friend
option_C: A unique, long passphrase for each important account
option_D: Special characters in a short word
rationale: Length beats cleverness, and reuse is the real enemy.

stem: Why is reusing a password the real problem?
option_A: When one site is hacked, stolen email and password lists are tried on other sites, so one leak can open every account that shares the key
option_B: Hackers cannot guess reused passwords
option_C: Websites cannot store reused passwords
option_D: Reuse makes a password shorter
rationale: The Key Ring idea: one key for six doors means six open doors after a leak.
kit_source: Academy Module 2, 'Why reuse is the problem'

stem: What does Module 2 say about a login code a service sends you?
option_A: It is safe to share if the person sounds friendly
option_B: A moderator may need it to fix your account
option_C: A code is a key: nobody who is really helping you will ask you to read it to them
option_D: Support staff may ask for it to verify you
rationale: Even a code from a text message can be tricked out of you. The rule holds for support, friends and moderators.

stem: Why does Module 2 advise turning on 2-step verification for email first?
option_A: Email can reset many other accounts, so it is the master key
option_B: Email accounts do not have passwords
option_C: Email stores the most photos
option_D: Email is the only account that can be hacked
rationale: Protect the account that can unlock the others.
kit_source: Academy Module 2, 2-step verification rules; self-check Q3

stem: What is a passkey?
option_A: A code texted to your phone
option_B: A password manager's master phrase
option_C: A cryptographic key on your device unlocked by fingerprint, face or screen lock, replacing a typed password
option_D: A longer password written on paper
rationale: Nothing to type and nothing to hand over in a phishing message. Support varies by service, and recovery needs planning.

stem: Why can a passkey resist a phishing message?
option_A: It expires every hour
option_B: There is nothing to type or hand over, and the key only works for the real site on your device
option_C: It is stored in plain text where fake sites cannot see it
option_D: It is a very long password
rationale: The kit's description: nothing to copy and nothing to reuse. NIST treats such authenticators as phishing resistant.
kit_source: Academy Module 2, Passkeys; Fact-Check Report Round 1, item 6.5

stem: Which invented passphrase best fits the kit's rule of thumb?
option_A: Tr0ub4dor&3
option_B: P@ssw0rd!
option_C: violet anchor pencil toast marble
option_D: Fluffy2012
rationale: Five unrelated words, over 15 characters, silly and memorable. The others are short, common patterns or famous substitutions.
kit_source: Academy Module 2, 'What makes a good password'

stem: What does NIST SP 800-63B-4 say about forcing regular password changes, as summarized in the kit?
option_A: Passwords must be changed every 30 days
option_B: Verifiers must not require periodic changes without evidence of compromise
option_C: Changes are required only for children
option_D: Passwords must change after every login
rationale: The kit cites the current revision (Aug 2025): no composition rules, no routine periodic changes, a blocklist check, and at least 64 characters allowed.
kit_source: Academy Module 2, Part 1; Fact-Check Report Round 1, item 6.1

stem: Which are the five hackles-raisers taught for phishing and scams?
option_A: Spelling, color, logo, font and length
option_B: Urgency, secrecy, too good to be true, the ask, and does not add up
option_C: Speed, price, brand, color and sound
option_D: Sender, subject, date, size and language
rationale: None of the five depends on technology, so they travel across apps.

stem: A message says, 'Your account will be deleted in 1 hour. Click to confirm your password.' Which hackles-raisers are present?
option_A: Secrecy only
option_B: Urgency and the ask
option_C: None of them
option_D: Too good to be true only
rationale: A deadline is urgency and a request to confirm a password is the ask. Pause and check another way.

stem: What is the Own-Door rule in the Facilitator Kit?
option_A: Reply to the sender and ask if it is real
option_B: Do not use the link, number or contact in the message; open the site or app yourself, call a number you already had, or ask in person
option_C: Click the link only if it looks professional
option_D: Forward the message to a friend to check
rationale: Check another way, using a door you already trust.
kit_source: Facilitator Kit Handout H4; Academy Module 2

stem: A student tells you she typed her game password into a fake giveaway page. Which response fits the kit?
option_A: 'Thank you for telling me. It is not your fault. Let's tell a trusted adult and use the official steps to secure the account.'
option_B: 'Don't tell anyone; we will fix it quietly.'
option_C: 'How could you be so careless?'
option_D: 'Never play that game again.'
rationale: Shame-free, tell an adult, official recovery. Blame makes the next disclosure less likely.

stem: Why does the kit say 'Never share personal information online' is not enough on its own?
option_A: It is a complete safety plan
option_B: It is illegal advice
option_C: It is vague and cannot be followed perfectly, so it should be paired with 'who is asking, why, and tell a trusted adult'
option_D: It applies only to adults
rationale: The kit frames a better rule: who is asking, why, and do I trust them, plus telling.
kit_source: Academy Module 2, 'A privacy rule that does not work'

stem: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule say?
option_A: Three passwords, two locks, one code
option_B: Three copies, on two kinds of storage, with one stored elsewhere
option_C: Three devices, two accounts, one email
option_D: Three updates a year, two restarts, one backup
rationale: The kit adds that backups should be tested, and for most teachers an approved cloud plus a second location is enough.
kit_source: Academy Module 2, Part 5; Concepts Lab Demo 10

stem: Why does Demo 10 stress restoring a backup at least once?
option_A: Backups only work if restored weekly
option_B: Restoring makes files smaller
option_C: Restoring deletes the backup
option_D: A tested copy kept elsewhere beats panic; a copy you have never restored is only a hope
rationale: The big idea is another copy, somewhere else, that you know works.

stem: What is the 'mosaic effect' in Demo 9?
option_A: Small, harmless facts combine into a picture that points to one person
option_B: An image filter
option_C: A password made of tiles
option_D: A map of Wi-Fi coverage
rationale: Alone one footprint rarely matters; together they form a profile. The demo uses a fictional person, Quinn.

stem: Which three families of proof does Demo 6 use for authentication?
option_A: A name, an address and a phone number
option_B: Something you type, click and send
option_C: Something you know, something you have, something you are
option_D: A username, a nickname and a code word
rationale: A second proof from a different family stops most takeovers from a stolen password alone.

stem: What does Demo 7 teach about updates?
option_A: Updates make old holes larger
option_B: Updates only add new features
option_C: Updates are optional for security
option_D: An update is a fix for a known hole, and the race is between the fix reaching devices and someone misusing the hole
rationale: Software has mistakes; some are holes. Every copy needs the fix.
kit_source: Concepts Lab Demo 7; Academy Module 2 Part 4; self-check Q7

stem: Why do well-built sites store a hash (a one-way fingerprint) of a password instead of the password?
option_A: It lets staff read passwords more easily
option_B: The site can check what you type without keeping it, and a stolen list of fingerprints is much less harmful than a stolen list of passwords
option_C: It makes login slower on purpose for every user
option_D: Hashes can be reversed instantly to show the password
rationale: Demo 2's big idea is the one-way fingerprint. Salting and slow hashes are taught at the 9-12 level.

stem: The kit says 'at least 15 characters (CISA recommends 16 or more)'. Why are both numbers there?
option_A: Both numbers are guesses
option_B: 15 is for children and 16 is for adults
option_C: The two agencies disagree and the kit picked one at random
option_D: NIST sets 15 as the minimum for a password used alone, while CISA recommends at least 16 characters or 5 to 7 unrelated words
rationale: Round 1 corrected the earlier rule to reflect both sources.

stem: A slide says 'MFA blocks over 99 percent of attacks, says Microsoft.' How should it be handled?
option_A: Raise it to 100 percent for emphasis
option_B: Delete all mention of MFA
option_C: Present it as a proven national statistic
option_D: Label it as a vendor claim (99.9 percent of account compromise attacks, 2019, citing a SANS white paper), indicative not exact, and note CISA gives no percentage
rationale: Round 1 corrected the wording and kept the caution.
kit_source: Fact-Check Report Round 1, item 6.3; Concepts Lab Demo 6

stem: A colleague wants to paste a student's name and a disclosure note into a chatbot to tidy the wording. What does the kit say?
option_A: Do not paste student names, work containing personal details or disclosure notes into a chatbot, and follow your district's AI policy [VERIFY]
option_B: It is fine if the chatbot is popular
option_C: It is fine if the name is shortened to initials
option_D: It is fine for notes, but not for names
rationale: Module 3 sets this limit for teacher use of AI tools. Student data and disclosures stay out of chatbots.
kit_source: Academy Module 3, 'A note on teacher use'

stem: Which four patterns does Module 3 teach as showing up in every app?
option_A: Speed, Cost, Volume, Size
option_B: Pressure, Secrecy, The Ask, The Move
option_C: Name, Age, Place, School
option_D: Games, Chats, Video, Feeds
rationale: Every risk in Module 1 is a variation on these four.

stem: Which pairing of pattern and response is correct?
option_A: Secrecy: Pause. The Ask: Tell. Pressure: Check.
option_B: The Move: Click. The Ask: Reply. Secrecy: Share.
option_C: Secrecy: Tell. The Ask: Check. Pressure: Pause.
option_D: Pressure: Tell. Secrecy: Check. The Ask: Pause.
rationale: Pressure gets a Pause, secrecy gets a Tell, the ask gets a Check, and the move gets a Pause and a question about why the new place is more private.

stem: Which four adult reactions does Module 3 say make children stop telling?
option_A: Panic, punishment, lecture, minimizing
option_B: Delay, distraction, laughter and gifts
option_C: Phone calls, e-mails, texts and letters
option_D: Praise, thanks, questions and silence
rationale: Each ends the conversation. Take them off the table in advance with the promise: you will not be in trouble for telling me things.

stem: A student says, 'My friend got a weird message. What should she do?' What is the best reply?
option_A: 'Is it actually you?'
option_B: 'That sounds stressful. I'm glad your friend has someone like you. Here is what I would suggest for her... and you can always tell me about anything too.'
option_C: 'That is nothing to worry about.'
option_D: 'Tell your friend to stop using that app.'
rationale: Treat 'my friend' as real and keep the door open. Asking 'is it you?' can close it.
kit_source: Academy Module 3, 'When my friend means me'

stem: Which question is the best open question for a student about a game?
option_A: 'Do you play every night?'
option_B: 'Is that game safe?'
option_C: 'What do you like about it, and what is annoying?'
option_D: 'You are not talking to strangers, right?'
rationale: Open questions invite explanation. Yes and no questions and loaded questions end conversations.
kit_source: Academy Module 3, curiosity script; Module 5 Part 3

stem: Which AI companion idea is part of the kit's 'fact sheet, not a scare'?
option_A: It forgets everything you type
option_B: It can agree too much, so it is not a substitute for a trusted adult
option_C: It is a person on the other end
option_D: It is always a reliable source of facts
rationale: The kit lists: not a person, can be wrong, can agree too much, remembers and stores, not a substitute for a trusted adult.

stem: What did Pew Research Center report in December 2025 about US teens and AI chatbots?
option_A: 95 percent, about half daily
option_B: 64 percent say they use AI chatbots, about 3 in 10 daily
option_C: 99 percent, all daily
option_D: 14 percent, about 1 in 100 daily
rationale: [VERIFIED 2026-10-05 in the kit; 1,458 teens surveyed Sept 25 to Oct 9, 2025.]
kit_source: Academy Module 3, World 3; Fact-Check Report Round 1, item 4.16

stem: A speaker says 'one in three teens discuss serious matters with AI instead of a person.' What is wrong?
option_A: The statistic is correct as stated
option_B: Common Sense reported about one in three AI-companion users, not one in three of all teens
option_C: The true figure is one in three of all adults
option_D: Common Sense reported that nobody does this
rationale: The denominator matters. Round 1 corrected the kit on this point.

stem: Why does Module 3 say 'a group chat is not a private room'?
option_A: Anything can be screenshotted, forwarded or shown to others
option_B: Group chats are always public websites
option_C: Group chats delete messages automatically
option_D: Only teachers can see group chats
rationale: This is the key idea for children about group chats.

stem: A chat goes quiet whenever one student posts. Which upstander moves does the kit's 6-8 'Group Chat Dynamics' lesson practice?
option_A: Screenshotting and posting the chat publicly
option_B: Waiting to see what happens
option_C: Joining in so you are not the next target
option_D: A quiet check-in, saying 'not cool' in the chat, leaving the chat, and telling a trusted adult
rationale: These are the upstander moves named in Module 3.

stem: In Demo 12, what is the better habit than trying to spot a fake by its flaws?
option_A: Share it to see what others say
option_B: Trust any image that looks sharp
option_C: Decide it is fake because it is shocking
option_D: Verify the source: find the original, look for other reliable confirmation, and use a second channel for urgent requests
rationale: Fakes improve, so verification habits outlast flaw-spotting.

stem: What is the 'liar's dividend' in Demo 12?
option_A: Wrongly dismissing real evidence as fake because fakes exist
option_B: A tax on synthetic media
option_C: The profit made by deepfake apps
option_D: A reward for exposing fakes
rationale: Good defenders are careful, not cynical.

stem: A shocking photo of a public figure is spreading. What should a student do first, according to Demo 12 and the Assessment Pack?
option_A: Share it fast while it is trending
option_B: Check the original source and look for confirmation from reliable outlets before sharing
option_C: Decide it is real if it looks real
option_D: Decide it is fake because it is shocking
rationale: Both gut reactions skip checking. The Assessment Pack 9-12 survey item uses this answer key.
kit_source: Assessment Pack Section 6 item 7; Concepts Lab Demo 12

stem: What does Module 3 say about the research on screens and well-being?
option_A: It sets a single daily limit for everyone
option_B: It proves screens cause harm in all children
option_C: It is mixed and still developing; quality, content, context, sleep and what screens replace seem to matter more than a number on a clock
option_D: It proves screens have no effect
rationale: The kit points to the AAP's family media plan approach [VERIFIED 2026-10-05: healthychildren.org].

stem: A teacher tells students that several state attorneys general have 'proved' a game company harms children. How should this be corrected?
option_A: These are allegations and fast-moving developments, not settled findings, so do not state them as fact in class [VERIFY current status]
option_B: Say the actions were all dismissed
option_C: Remove the topic entirely and never discuss games
option_D: Add that the companies have admitted guilt
rationale: Module 3 and the evidence file label them allegations.
kit_source: Academy Module 3, World 1; Evidence file Section 2.6

stem: In Week 4's Curiosity Interview, which behavior fits the five-step script?
option_A: Correcting the partner's app choices
option_B: Listening about 70 percent of the time and reflecting back what you heard without judging
option_C: Writing down names and details to keep
option_D: Offering a lecture on risks
rationale: Be curious, listen more than you talk, reflect back, ask open questions, offer do not impose.

stem: What is Rule 1 of the five rules of safety teaching that works?
option_A: Skills over information
option_B: Information over skills
option_C: Fear over calm
option_D: Assemblies over lessons
rationale: Good lessons teach a few facts and one concrete skill to practice.

stem: Which is a skill-based objective (the 'Teacher test')?
option_A: After this, students will appreciate security
option_B: After this, students will know that passwords are important
option_C: After this, students will be aware of hackers
option_D: After this, students can say 'No, I'll check with my grown-up' when someone asks for a password
rationale: A skill is a verb students can show. Know, be aware and appreciate cannot be observed.

stem: Why does role-play work for safety skills?
option_A: It tests children on facts
option_B: It replaces the need to tell an adult
option_C: It scares children into compliance
option_D: It makes the words available when the real moment comes; a child who has practiced 'I need help' can say it once in a hard moment
rationale: Practice builds a reflex.

stem: Which role-play practice does Module 4 recommend?
option_A: Assign the most shy student to play the victim
option_B: Ask students to act out graphic details
option_C: Let students play the helper, not the victim, and have the adult play the difficult person with a clear signal for stepping out of character
option_D: Use real stories from students
rationale: Also use puppets or character cards for younger children so no child plays the 'bad guy.'

stem: Which framing replaces a fear message with a tool?
option_A: 'If you talk to a stranger, something terrible could happen.'
option_B: 'If anyone asks for secrets or pictures, your hackles go up. Pause and tell.'
option_C: 'Your life will be ruined.'
option_D: 'You will be hacked!'
rationale: The Hackles framing gives a signal and an action.

stem: Which three promises does Hackles language make?
option_A: Nobody will ever know; nothing will happen; everything is private
option_B: You will always be right; you can never be fooled; you must never share
option_C: Every answer will be graded; every mistake is recorded; every parent is told
option_D: A false alarm is fine and welcome; it is never your fault; you will not be in trouble for telling
rationale: Say them aloud often, especially to older students, who assume the opposite.

stem: Which phrase best replaces 'Why did you click it?'
option_A: 'You should have known better.'
option_B: 'Good kids do not do that.'
option_C: 'What happened next?'
option_D: 'How could you?'
rationale: 'Why' questions can sound like blame.

stem: Why does the kit say 'never' language invites failure?
option_A: Adults should say 'always' instead
option_B: Children inevitably share some things, so 'never share your name' sets them up to feel they failed; 'think first' and 'check first' are more honest
option_C: Children are not capable of safe behavior
option_D: 'Never' is too gentle for safety lessons
rationale: Prefer 'think first,' 'ask a trusted adult,' 'check first.'

stem: What is a spiral curriculum, as used in Hackles?
option_A: Repeating the identical lesson every year
option_B: Each grade band returns to the same core routine and strands at a more advanced level
option_C: Teaching only the newest apps
option_D: Teaching all topics in one long unit
rationale: One lesson does not do it; revisit a little deeper over months and years.

stem: Two grade 4 password lessons are compared. Which is the good lesson?
option_A: The teacher reads ten password rules from slides and gives a quiz
option_B: The teacher warns that bad passwords will cost students everything
option_C: The teacher assigns a chapter on password history
option_D: Groups build the funniest four-word passphrase, then use a crack-timer card; exit ticket asks for a new rule and when to tell a grown-up
rationale: The good lesson has students create, compare, discuss and decide in a calm tone.

stem: Two grade 8 lessons on pressure online: A shows graphic stories of what happens to children who share pictures; B uses calm case files about a fictional character and rehearses STOP, SAVE, TELL, REPORT. Which statement is correct?
option_A: A is better because it motivates through fear
option_B: B follows the evidence-informed approach: no graphic detail, a skill, and help-seeking, while A risks shame, fear and silence
option_C: A is better because it is more realistic
option_D: Both are equally good
rationale: The kit's Good versus Weak pair says exactly this.

stem: Which item is on the 'good lesson' checklist?
option_A: Gives students a role other than victim
option_B: Includes a graphic example for realism
option_C: Requires every student to share a personal story
option_D: Runs 45 minutes
rationale: Also: one clear skill, a rehearsal, no fear or shame, ends with who to tell, about 15 minutes, a check, a safe way to disclose.

stem: What caution does Module 4 give about gamification?
option_A: Use games that practice the skill, never games that act out the harm
option_B: Never use games
option_C: Games should be graded
option_D: Use points to rank children against each other
rationale: Fun matters, and the game must teach the skill.

stem: A colleague says, 'Can't we just show a video? Fear gets attention.' What is the best reply?
option_A: A video alone is information; add a short rehearsal and a calm tone, because fear without a skill is just fear and shame blocks telling
option_B: Say a video is the same as an active lesson
option_C: Agree, because attention is the main goal
option_D: Say videos are always banned
rationale: The kit's rules favor rehearsal and calm skill practice. A video can serve as a hook only.
kit_source: Academy Module 4, Scenario 4.A and Rules 1 to 3

stem: A student who 'already knows it all' keeps interrupting. What does the kit suggest?
option_A: Quiz them in front of the class
option_B: Send them out of the room
option_C: Ignore them for the rest of the term
option_D: Give them a role, such as a helper, detective or demonstrator
rationale: Module 5's management table says to give know-it-alls and jokers a role.

stem: During a role-play, several students giggle. Which response fits?
option_A: Cancel the lesson
option_B: Name it kindly ('A lot of us laugh when things feel awkward') and keep going
option_C: Single out one student
option_D: Stop and punish the class
rationale: Giggling is often nervous energy, not disrespect.

stem: In the student plan STOP, SAVE, TELL, REPORT, what does SAVE mean?
option_A: Save and share any image as proof
option_B: Save the password to a document
option_C: Delete everything to be safe
option_D: Keep the account name, links, dates and text threats; never save or share images
rationale: SAVE means text evidence only.

stem: Why does Module 4 prefer 'someone who is pressuring you' to 'predator' and 'the person it happened to' to 'victim' when talking with children?
option_A: The words are too long
option_B: The words are more frightening
option_C: Shame-free, concrete language is easier for children to act on and keeps telling safe
option_D: The words are legally prohibited in classrooms
rationale: The language table lists 'predator' and 'victim' (to a child) as phrases to avoid.

stem: What are the four parts of a 15-minute Hackles lesson and their times?
option_A: Hook 2, Activity 8, Discuss 3, Takeaway 2
option_B: Lecture 10, Quiz 3, Homework 1, Test 1
option_C: Hook 5, Activity 5, Discuss 3, Takeaway 2
option_D: Video 5, Video 5, Video 3, Video 2
rationale: The same skeleton is used in every Teacher Guide.

stem: What does 'one skill, one phrase, one gesture' mean?
option_A: One teacher, one student, one device
option_B: Three separate lessons in one
option_C: One fact, one date, one quiz
option_D: A lesson should be summarized by a single skill, a repeatable sentence and a hand signal; more means it is probably two lessons
rationale: Examples: Pause before you click; 'Hackles up? Pause, Check, Tell'; Pause Palm.

stem: Why must the Hook stay at about two minutes?
option_A: If you are still talking at minute three, you have lost the class, and the activity is where students learn
option_B: Hooks are not allowed to be fun
option_C: The Takeaway needs 8 minutes
option_D: Students cannot listen for more than a minute
rationale: Hook rules: do not scare, do not exceed two minutes, say what you will practice.

stem: Which order lists the question ladder from lower to higher level?
option_A: Apply, recall, evaluate, create, explain
option_B: Explain, recall, create, apply, evaluate
option_C: Recall, explain, apply, evaluate, create
option_D: Create, evaluate, apply, explain, recall
rationale: Start with what did we notice and climb toward how could we improve it.

stem: Which question is open rather than closed?
option_A: 'Is that right?'
option_B: 'Was that a scam?'
option_C: 'What made you think it was a scam?'
option_D: 'Did you tell an adult?'
rationale: Open questions invite explanation.

stem: A student says, 'I would just send it.' What is the best response?
option_A: Ignore the comment
option_B: 'That is a terrible idea.'
option_C: Ask the student to explain in front of everyone why they are careless
option_D: 'Thanks for being honest. Lots of people feel that pressure. Let's practice a different response,' then follow up privately
rationale: A worrying answer is information, not a reason to shame.

stem: How long should wait time be after asking a question?
option_A: 30 seconds
option_B: Under one second
option_C: About 3 to 5 seconds
option_D: Two minutes
rationale: Wait time raises quality and participation.

stem: What is the purpose of the pass card?
option_A: It preserves safety and dignity: any student may say 'pass' without explaining
option_B: It lets students skip lessons
option_C: It excuses students from homework
option_D: It records who is uncomfortable
rationale: Always available, especially in sensitive lessons.

stem: You are 12 minutes in and the activity is not finished. What does the time rescue table say?
option_A: Add a second activity
option_B: Skip the takeaway
option_C: Extend the lesson by 10 minutes
option_D: Cut one round of practice; keep the takeaway and the open door
rationale: Never cut the takeaway and the open door.

stem: Which is one of the 'four mistakes to avoid above all'?
option_A: Giving students a role
option_B: Promising secrecy
option_C: Starting with a hook
option_D: Using a hand signal
rationale: The four: making a child the example, promising secrecy, ignoring the open door, teaching without prep for disclosures.

stem: A student starts a long personal story in front of the class. What do you do?
option_A: Let the story continue so everyone learns
option_B: Tell them to stop and not speak again
option_C: Ask follow-up questions in front of the class
option_D: Thank them, redirect gently ('let's keep the details between us and talk privately after'), and follow up that day
rationale: This protects the student's privacy and keeps a path open for disclosure.

stem: What is the Takeaway formula?
option_A: Fact plus quiz plus score
option_B: Story plus joke plus video
option_C: Skill plus gesture plus promise
option_D: Warning plus consequence plus rule
rationale: Example: Pause before you click (Pause Palm), plus 'a false alarm is fine and it is never your fault.'

stem: In the Micro-Teach Rubric, which total marks Hackles-Ready practice?
option_A: 6 to 11
option_C: 18 to 24 out of 24
option_D: Only 24
rationale: Six rows scored 1 to 4: 6 to 11 keep practicing; 12 to 17 solid; 18 to 24 Hackles-Ready.

stem: Only five students are active during the 8-minute activity. Which rubric row and design rule does this violate?
option_A: Active practice: every student should do the skill at least twice, so redesign the activity
option_B: Skill focus: the skill is unnamed
option_C: Safety and closure: the close was calm
option_D: Tone and language: no shaming occurred
rationale: The activity design rule is that everyone does something.
kit_source: Academy Module 5, The Activity; rubric row 3

stem: A student's exit ticket says, 'Something happened on my account and I don't want to say.' What is the right step?
option_A: Read exit tickets the same day, treat it as a possible disclosure, follow the First 10 Minutes and your policy, and involve the counselor
option_B: Contact the family first without checking policy
option_C: Post the note on the board to ask who wrote it
option_D: Wait until the end of term to read the exit tickets
rationale: Module 5 says to check exit tickets for worrying content on the same day.

stem: What is the 'I do, we do, you do' pattern?
option_A: Students teach, teacher watches, parents grade
option_B: Teacher models, the class tries together, then pairs or groups practice twice
option_C: Teacher talks, class listens, class takes a test
option_D: Teacher reads, students copy, students sign
rationale: Typical timing: 1 minute I do, 2 minutes we do, 5 minutes you do.

stem: Which hook follows Module 5's hook rules?
option_A: A three-minute statistics lecture
option_B: 'Imagine something terrible happens to you online.'
option_C: Hold up a fake pop-up card and ask for a thumbs up or down: 'Detectives, is this real?'
option_D: A graphic news story about a victim
rationale: A good hook is curious, calm, short and names the skill. It never scares.

stem: The Peer Coaching Guide says not to add up Fun, Safe, Skill-based ratings or compare teachers. Why?
option_A: Because the ratings are always wrong
option_B: Because totals are required by law
option_C: Because teachers should never be observed
option_D: A rating is a conversation starter, not a grade; patterns matter more than single items, and only one grow is given
rationale: The guide says to pick one grow and avoid comparing teachers.

stem: Which three sentences does the kit teach for the first moments of a disclosure?
option_A: 'I won't tell anyone. It will be fine. Forget it.'
option_B: 'Are you sure? That is odd. Delete it.'
option_C: 'Thank you for telling me. This is not your fault. You are not in trouble.'
option_D: 'Why did you do that? Who else knows? Show me.'
rationale: The three sentences reassure without blame.
kit_source: Academy Module 6, Part 3; Disclosure Guide Section 2

stem: What is the teacher's role in a disclosure?
option_A: Counselor who treats the child
option_B: Detective who confronts the other person
option_C: Recognition and response: listen, reassure, protect evidence safely, report, hand off, document, and look after the child and yourself
option_D: Investigator who finds out what happened
rationale: You are not an investigator, a therapist or a police officer.

stem: Why should you not promise a child 'I won't tell anyone'?
option_A: Because teachers are not allowed to speak to children privately
option_B: Because children do not care about secrecy
option_C: Because secrets are always safe to keep
option_D: You may be required to tell people whose job is to help, and breaking a promise hurts more; say 'I can't keep this a secret, because I want to get you help. I will tell you who I tell.'
rationale: Honesty about limits builds trust.
kit_source: Academy Module 6, Part 3 Step 4; Script D

stem: A second grader says, 'Somebody on my tablet game said not to tell my mom. He gives me gems.' What is the best response?
option_A: 'Show me the chat.'
option_B: 'He is probably just a kind player.'
option_C: 'Thank you for telling me. You are not in trouble. Can you tell me a little more?' Then report on reasonable suspicion without asking for names or details
option_D: Phone the child's mother before anyone else
rationale: Secrecy and gifts from an unknown person are a reasonable-suspicion pattern. Do not interrogate, and do not contact the family first.
kit_source: Academy Module 6, Script A and debrief

stem: What is the typical standard that triggers a report, as described in the kit?
option_A: A police report
option_B: A confession
option_C: Reasonable suspicion or reason to believe, not proof; the exact standard varies by state [VERIFY]
option_D: Proof beyond doubt
rationale: Reporters do not have to prove abuse occurred.
kit_source: Academy Module 6, Part 2; Fact-Check Report Round 1, item 3.3

stem: Why does the kit say that telling your principal may not satisfy your own duty?
option_A: The duty is identical in every state
option_B: Principals are never involved in reporting
option_C: Teachers are never legally required to report
option_D: In many states the duty is personal and internal reporting may not relieve it, while procedures vary by state; check your state and district policy [VERIFY]
rationale: Round 1 corrected 'most states' to 'many states.' The practical message is to report yourself and also tell the administrator per policy.
kit_source: Fact-Check Report Round 1, item 3.4; Academy Module 6 Part 2

stem: What must you never do with suspected sexual images of a minor?
option_A: Keep them to show to the principal
option_B: Forward them to the counselor
option_C: View, copy, download, forward, print or screenshot them
option_D: Print one copy for the file
rationale: Under federal law, knowing possession or sharing is a serious crime with narrow defenses; secure the device per policy [counsel to confirm].
kit_source: Academy Module 6, Step 5; Disclosure Guide Step 5

stem: A student says a classmate has an intimate image on a phone. A colleague suggests you 'just look to check.' What do you do?
option_A: Delete the image to protect the classmate
option_B: Look briefly to confirm
option_C: Ask another student to forward it to you
option_D: Do not look; ask the student not to delete or forward anything; secure the device per policy; report personally and promptly
rationale: Good intentions are not a safe assumption. Authorities collect evidence lawfully.

stem: In STOP, SAVE, TELL, REPORT, what is saved?
option_A: The password to the account
option_B: Nothing; everything is deleted
option_C: Account names, profile links, dates and threatening text, never images
option_D: Copies of any image sent
rationale: SAVE means text evidence.
kit_source: Academy Module 6, Part 4; Assessment Pack Section 6

stem: What does NCMEC's Take It Down service do, according to the kit?
option_A: Reports the child to the school
option_B: Removes any adult image from any site instantly
option_C: Deletes a child's account
option_D: Helps remove images of people who were under 18 when the image was made from participating platforms, using a hash so the image is never uploaded. It does not work on encrypted platforms
rationale: People 18 or older are directed to StopNCII.org. [VERIFIED 2026-10-05: takeitdown.ncmec.org]
kit_source: Fact-Check Report Round 1, items 1.2 and 1.6; Academy Module 6

stem: Which entry belongs in your documentation of a disclosure?
option_A: Your guess about what really happened
option_B: An opinion about the family
option_C: A diagnosis
option_D: The child's exact words in quotation marks, date, time, place, who you told and what you did
rationale: Document facts only.

stem: Where should a private conversation with a child take place?
option_A: In a car
option_B: Alone in a closed room
option_C: A private place that is still visible to other adults, with the door open or a glass window; never alone behind a closed door
option_D: In front of the class
rationale: This protects the child and the adult.

stem: A student blurts out in class, 'That happened to me!' about a threat and a picture. What is the best immediate response?
option_A: Ignore it until the lesson ends tomorrow
option_B: Ask them for details in front of the class
option_C: Let classmates ask questions
option_D: Thank them, say you will talk privately in a moment, calm the class and arrange for another adult to supervise, then meet the student that day
rationale: Contain the moment without shaming, protect privacy, and move to the First 10 Minutes.
kit_source: Academy Module 6, Script C and 'Disclosures in front of the class'

stem: After a lesson on pressure online, a student says, 'It's kind of me.' after speaking of 'a friend.' What now?
option_A: 'Why did you not say so?'
option_B: Promise to tell nobody
option_C: Thank them calmly, say the three sentences, be honest about telling people who can help, and do not ask to see messages or images
option_D: 'I knew it was you.'
rationale: Accept the shift calmly. Honest limits and no pressure.

stem: A student asks, 'Promise you won't tell?' Which reply is best?
option_A: 'Only if it is minor.'
option_B: 'I promise.'
option_C: 'I want to hear it. If it is about someone being hurt or in danger, I must get help from others. I will tell you who and why, and I will not go behind your back.'
option_D: 'I can't promise anything and I do not want to hear it.'
rationale: It is honest and kind and leaves the door open; promising secrecy and then breaking it harms trust.

stem: Which crisis resources does the kit list for young people and adults?
option_A: A school email alias
option_B: 211 and 311 only
option_C: 988 (call or text), Crisis Text Line (text HOME to 741741), and NCMEC CyberTipline (1-800-843-5678; report.cybertip.org)
option_D: The police non-emergency line only
rationale: [VERIFIED 2026-10-05: 988lifeline.org, crisistextline.org, report.cybertip.org]. Call 911 for immediate danger.

stem: A parent phones and says, 'My daughter told me she told you something. What did she say?' What is the best response?
option_A: Say you cannot talk to parents at all
option_B: Repeat what the daughter said
option_C: Stay warm and share no details, connect them to the counselor, tell your administrator, and consider whether a family member could be involved before sharing anything
option_D: Tell the parent to ask a friend
rationale: Follow policy and involve the counselor.

stem: What is secondary traumatic stress, in plain language?
option_A: Hearing about a child's hard experience can affect you even though you were not there; it is common and does not mean you did something wrong [VERIFY with a mental health source if cited]
option_B: A form of blame
option_C: A sign that you should not teach any topic
option_D: A condition only counselors get
rationale: Care plan layers: right after, same day, that evening, that week, longer term.

stem: Which statement is a phrase to avoid in a disclosure, and why?
option_A: 'I believe you.' It is too short
option_B: 'Your parents will be so upset.' It adds fear
option_C: 'Thank you for telling me.' It is a form of praise
option_D: 'What would help you feel safest?' It is leading
rationale: The avoid list also includes why questions, shock, 'I won't tell anyone,' 'I'm sure it's fine,' 'Let me see,' and 'Are you sure?'

stem: For a cyberbullying incident without sexual content or a threat, which steps does the Disclosure Guide list?
option_A: Support the child targeted, help them save text evidence, document, report within bullying policy, avoid face-to-face mediation, support the child who was unkind, and check in at a day, a week and a month
option_B: Put both children together immediately to settle it
option_C: Post the incident in a staff chat
option_D: Delete all messages
rationale: Do not mediate in a way that re-harms.

stem: Which of these needs immediate escalation to an administrator and counselor?
option_A: A game score argument
option_B: A late assignment
option_C: A mean nickname used once
option_D: Threats of violence, self-harm statements, sexual content, doxxing, or a child saying they feel unsafe at school or home
rationale: These are the red flags listed in the bullying section.

stem: You are not sure whether a student's comment is reportable. What does the kit advise?
option_A: Wait a week to see if more details appear
option_B: Ask the student's friends
option_C: Question the student until sure
option_D: Report if you are unsure, because the standard is suspicion not certainty; ask your administrator or the CPS hotline but do not delay while waiting
rationale: The threshold is reasonable suspicion, not proof.

stem: When should you not contact the family first?
option_A: Never; always call the family first
option_B: Only if the child is over 12
option_C: Whenever a child is upset
option_D: If a family member could be involved, the child asks you not to out of fear for their safety, or authorities advise otherwise
rationale: Follow district policy and CPS or law enforcement guidance.
kit_source: Disclosure Guide Step 6; Academy Module 6 Step 6

stem: Which are the five principles for every lesson in Module 7?
option_A: Many ways in; no one is singled out; everyone has someone; assume good intentions in families; safety first, always
option_B: One way in; call on volunteers; public sharing; family contact; lecture
option_C: Speed; volume; testing; ranking; grading
option_D: Fear; rules; secrecy; penalty; reward
rationale: Inclusion never lowers safeguards.

stem: A child needs to disclose, and a classmate offers to translate. What do you do?
option_A: Ask the child to write in English
option_B: Do not use a classmate or sibling; offer a drawing or note in any language, a trusted bilingual adult or an interpreter service
option_C: Accept the classmate as interpreter
option_D: Delay the conversation
rationale: Children should not interpret for sensitive conversations.

stem: Why does the kit say a bilingual buddy should be a choice and rotate?
option_A: So no child becomes the permanent translator or is put on the spot
option_B: Because translation is illegal
option_C: Because buddies are never helpful
option_D: Because it gives extra points
rationale: Pairing is a support, not an obligation.

stem: A newcomer to the class cannot read an English poster about 'hackles.' What helps?
option_A: Ask the student to sit out
option_B: Pictures, gestures and the four hand signals, pre-taught key words, and teaching 'I need help' in home languages, verified by a fluent speaker [VERIFY]
option_C: Simplify by removing all safety content
option_D: Assign a longer text
rationale: Hand signals do not depend on English.

stem: What does Module 7 say about low-internet and no-device homes?
option_A: Exclude those students from the lesson
option_B: Assign online homework anyway
option_C: Treat low-device homes as a problem to fix
option_D: Do practice in class, never assign tasks needing a device at home, and remember low-device does not mean low-risk
rationale: The kit is unplugged by default.

stem: Which are the six trauma-informed practices in Module 7?
option_A: Predictability, choice, safety, calm closings, warmth and respect, collaboration
option_B: Fear, secrecy, humor, argument, debate, volume
option_C: Testing, grading, sorting, ranking, shaming, timing
option_D: Speed, surprise, rank, reward, penalty, silence
rationale: Reactions that look like misbehavior may be coping.

stem: Which phrase helps in a trauma-informed classroom?
option_A: 'Everyone else can do it.'
option_B: 'Just get over it.'
option_C: 'Stop being dramatic.'
option_D: 'You have choices. Take the time you need. It is okay to pass.'
rationale: The harmful list includes 'You are fine' and 'Why do you always...'.

stem: A student laughs and withdraws during a heavy topic. What does the kit suggest?
option_A: Ignore all behavior
option_B: It may be coping; respond with calm and curiosity, then check in privately
option_C: Discipline immediately
option_D: Call the family at once
rationale: Reactions that look like misbehavior may be a child coping with a heavy topic.

stem: What does L.E.A.R.N. stand for?
option_A: Look, Explain, Argue, Reply, Notify
option_B: Leave, End, Avoid, Refuse, Never
option_C: Listen, Empathize, Agree where you can, Respond with facts and options, Next step
option_D: Learn, Educate, Assess, Review, Navigate
rationale: A five-step response to parent pushback.

stem: A parent says, 'You are putting ideas in their heads.' Which reply fits?
option_A: 'That is a thoughtful worry. The lessons avoid graphic detail and give children tools; they usually meet these things online already' [VERIFY any research cited]
option_B: 'Our principal decided; I cannot discuss it.'
option_C: 'You are wrong, and the statistics prove it.'
option_D: 'Your child will be fine, so do not worry.'
rationale: Respond with facts and options, not an argument.

stem: A parent asks, 'Why are you collecting data on my child?' What is the accurate answer for a class using Hackles?
option_A: 'Hackles itself collects no student accounts or data. Any tally I keep is class-level and follows district policy.'
option_B: 'We cannot tell you.'
option_C: 'The company stores names for ten years.'
option_D: 'We collect everything for research.'
rationale: Hackles collects no student accounts and no student data; teachers keep paper, local, short-lived tallies per district policy [VERIFY].

stem: A family member could be involved in a child's disclosure. Which message to the family is appropriate?
option_A: A message copying the child's words
option_B: None until you have followed the Disclosure Guide and your policy; do not use a routine concern message
option_C: A call to the family before reporting
option_D: A warm routine message describing the concern
rationale: Sharing news of a concern applies to small, non-urgent matters only.

stem: What is the counselor's role in Parent Night?
option_A: To grade parents
option_B: To speak about what to do when a child tells you something hard and to help families pick a code word
option_C: To avoid answering questions
option_D: To take attendance
rationale: In the 30-minute script the counselor voice leads 'When your child tells you something hard.'

stem: A family wants to opt a child out of a higher-care lesson. What is the kit's approach?
option_A: Thank them; families can opt a child out of specific lessons, and the counselor explains the process and the alternative activity
option_B: Make the child do the lesson online
option_C: Tell the child's peers
option_D: Refuse and require attendance
rationale: Respect the family and keep the child included in a safe alternative.
kit_source: Academy Module 7, Part 7; Principal Checklist Section 7

stem: An angry parent raises their voice during a meeting about the lessons. What should you do?
option_A: Match their volume
option_B: Stay calm, set a boundary ('I want to help, and I will continue this when we can talk calmly'), end the conversation, and tell your administrator
option_C: Promise to cancel the lessons
option_D: Argue the statistics
rationale: You do not need to absorb abuse.

stem: What does 'everyone has someone' mean in practice?
option_A: Every child must name a parent
option_B: Every child must have a phone
option_C: Make sure every child can name a safe adult, and that school helpers count
option_D: Every adult must be a counselor
rationale: Some children have no safe adult at home, so school helpers matter.

stem: In the Inclusion Audit, which step in a lesson plan should be flagged?
option_A: A step with a pass card
option_B: A step that uses a hand signal
option_C: A step with pictures
option_D: A step that assumes a device, a quiet home, fluent English, fine-motor skills or a grown-up at home
rationale: Circle it and write one alternative.
kit_source: Academy Module 7, Try This Now and Activity 7.1

stem: Which family message best matches the kit?
option_A: 'This will protect your child from online harm.'
option_B: 'We teach children skills, not fear. Your child will never be in trouble for telling. Lessons avoid graphic detail and collect no student accounts or data.'
option_C: 'Your child is at serious risk.'
option_D: 'The state requires this, so there is no choice.'
rationale: Three simple messages from Module 7. Avoid promises of prevention and avoid fear.

stem: What are Module 8's three questions to ask about teaching?
option_A: Is it graded? Is it published? Is it paid?
option_B: Did they learn? Would they act? Is it safe to tell?
option_C: Was it fun? Was it long? Was it cheap?
option_D: Who won? Who lost? Who left?
rationale: The third is the most important and hardest to measure.

stem: What is the Tell-Readiness indicator?
option_A: The share of students who give the best answer on the two or three core 'would you tell' items
option_B: The number of disclosures a teacher receives
option_C: The grade on the final exam
option_D: The number of students in class
rationale: It is the Assessment Pack's most meaningful number. Report it as a change in survey answers.
kit_source: Academy Module 8, Part 2; Assessment Pack Section 7

stem: Pre: 11 of 24 chose the best answer. Post: 17 of 22. What is the change in percentage points, rounded?
option_A: About +31 points (46 percent to 77 percent)
option_B: About +17 points
option_C: About +55 points
option_D: About +6 points
rationale: 11/24 is about 46 percent and 17/22 is about 77 percent. The kit's honest summary adds that class sizes differed slightly.

stem: Core items pre: 26 of 72; post: 51 of 72. What is the Tell-Readiness change?
option_A: From 36 percent to 71 percent, +35 percentage points
option_B: +71 points
option_C: +51 points
option_D: +25 points
rationale: 26/72 is about 36 percent and 51/72 is about 71 percent.

stem: Why may disclosures go up after lessons, according to the Assessment Pack?
option_A: Because the lessons cause more harm
option_B: Students feel safer to tell, which can be a sign the program is working; more or fewer disclosures does not map neatly to more or less harm
option_C: Because the survey is faulty
option_D: Because teachers invent them
rationale: Do not treat an increase in disclosures as a failure.

stem: Why does the kit say that with 24 students small changes may be noise?
option_A: One child is about 4 percentage points, so small shifts can come from a few students or chance
option_B: Surveys are never accurate
option_C: Percentages cannot be computed for 24
option_D: Statistics require 100 students
rationale: Treat results as signals, not proof.

stem: Which is the most honest claim for a report?
option_A: 'Research proves this works.'
option_B: 'More of my students said they would tell a trusted adult after the lessons (n = 24 matched pairs; no comparison group).'
option_C: 'My lessons prevented abuse.'
option_D: 'Our students are now safe from phishing.'
rationale: Report changes in survey answers, the number of students, and the lack of a comparison group.
kit_source: Academy Module 8, Honest claims; Assessment Pack Section 14 Step 8

stem: What can a pre/post survey without a comparison group not show?
option_A: Cause, real-world behavior, honest answers under pressure, long-term effects
option_B: How many students are in class
option_C: Which items were skipped
option_D: Whether the survey printed
rationale: Changes may reflect maturation, other lessons, news, repeated testing or chance.

stem: How small a subgroup should you avoid reporting, per the kit?
option_A: Fewer than 1,000
option_B: Fewer than 100
option_C: Any subgroup of any size
option_D: Fewer than about ten students, subject to your district's suppression rule [VERIFY]
rationale: Small groups may identify individuals.
kit_source: Academy Module 8, Part 1; Assessment Pack Step 9

stem: Matched pairs: 15 up, 7 same, 2 down among 24. Which statement fits the kit's example?
option_A: 'Everyone improved.'
option_B: 'Two students are failing.'
option_C: 'Most students (15 of 24) improved. A few (2) went down. We look at those who did not move and offer more practice.'
option_D: 'The program caused improvement in 15 students.'
rationale: Report counts and offer additional practice.

stem: What are the four pieces of the Academy capstone?
option_A: Exam; essay; poster; video
option_B: Lesson Plan and Micro-Teach Evidence; Response Readiness Pack; Inclusion and Family Pack; Action Plan and Reflection
option_C: Quiz; survey; ticket; tally
option_D: Letter; chart; form; slide
rationale: Together they provide evidence for all six competencies.

stem: What does the Academy require for Hackles-Ready on the capstone rubric?
option_A: Any three rows at 2
option_B: Row A only
option_C: At least five of six rows at 3 or above, no row at 1, and Row E (Respond) at 3 or above
option_D: All rows at 4
rationale: Row E must be at least Hackles-Ready because response readiness is the most important competency for child safety.

stem: Scores on the post survey went down. What does Scenario 8.A suggest?
option_A: Hide the results
option_B: Blame the students
option_C: Drop the program
option_D: Look at the answers before panicking; students may be more honest after learning, or the post survey may be harder; ask students safely what would make telling easier
rationale: A drop can occur by chance and is worth examining only if it appears across several classes.
kit_source: Academy Module 8, Scenario 8.A; Assessment Pack Step 6

stem: A principal says, 'Our measures say we are great, so we are done.' What is the best reply?
option_A: Thank them, note the limits of surveys (no comparison group, self-report), and continue with glow-and-grow, delayed post surveys and observation
option_B: Say all measures are useless
option_C: Publish a claim of effectiveness
option_D: Agree and stop measuring
rationale: Measures are signals for improvement. The Assessment Pack lists optional improvements such as a delayed post and a comparison group.
kit_source: Academy Module 8, Scenario 8.B; Assessment Pack Step 7

stem: What is the purpose of the teach-back?
option_A: To record the presenter
option_B: To check understanding and spread learning: you explain in your own words and the listener asks questions
option_C: To test the listener for mistakes
option_D: To grade the instructor
rationale: It works for children, colleagues and families.

stem: A teacher plans to add a survey item asking students whether they have ever been bullied online. What does the kit say?
option_A: It is fine if no names are used
option_B: It is fine if anonymous
option_C: Keep student surveys to knowledge, skills and confidence; items about a student's own experiences can fall under PPRA protected areas and need counsel, parental review and consent [COUNSEL TO CONFIRM]
option_D: It is fine if the teacher gives it in class
rationale: The kit warns that a survey on protected areas given by a school official is treated as required and needs written parental consent; an opt-out is not enough [VERIFIED 2026-10-05; re-verify].
